problem_text:
Дана разбитая на единичные клетки прямоугольная доска \(a\times b\), где \(a\) и \(b\) взаимно просты. В \(n\) клетках стоят метки; множество клеток с метками выбирается случайно и равновероятно среди всех \(n\)-элементных подмножеств клеток доски.

Из левой нижней клетки начинает двигаться фишка. За один ход она переходит в соседнюю по диагонали клетку. Изначально она идёт вверх-вправо. Если фишка должна выйти за границу доски, она отражается от стороны, как бильярдный шар, и продолжает движение по диагонали. Например, у правой границы при попытке выйти направо она просто окажется на одну клетку выше.

Фишка останавливается, когда впервые попадает в клетку с меткой.

Найдите математическое ожидание числа посещённых клеток, включая последнюю.

problem.solution:
Вместо того чтобы отражать фишку от краёв, будем каждый раз отражать саму доску. Тогда путь фишки превращается в движение по диагонали на бесконечной клетчатой плоскости.

У полученной клетчатой плоскости есть периоды \(2a\) по горизонтали и \(2b\) по вертикали, поэтому достаточно следить за координатой фишки по модулю \(2a\) и \(2b\).

Покажем, что до первого повторения фишка проходит все \(ab\) клеток исходной доски. Пусть две посещённые клетки совпали раньше, обозначим эти моменты за \(k<\ell\). Совпадение означает, что по каждой координате мы попали либо в ту же копию, либо в отражённую. Поэтому для горизонтали имеем одно из двух:
\[
k\equiv\ell\pmod{2a}
\]
или
\[
k+\ell\equiv-1\pmod{2a},
\]
и для вертикали — то же самое по модулю \(2b\).

Если в обеих координатах выбран один и тот же тип совпадения, то либо \(\ell-k\), либо \(\ell+k+1\) кратно \(2ab\). Но
\[
0<\ell-k<\ell+k+1<2ab.
\]
Если типы разные, то легко получить противоречие по чётности. Тогда за первые \(ab\) шагов мы пройдём все клетки.

Значит, фишка задаёт некоторый порядок всех клеток доски:
\[
C_1,C_2,\ldots,C_{ab}.
\]
Метки стоят в случайных \(n\) клетках, то есть в этом порядке случайно выбраны \(n\) позиций из \(1,\ldots,ab\). Фишка остановится на первой из этих позиций, осталось найти математическое ожидание минимума.

Добавим специальное число \(0\) в начало и расположим полученные \(ab+1\) чисел по кругу. Минимум выбранных чисел — это длина промежутка после \(0\) до первой выбранной точки. По симметрии средняя длина каждого из \(n+1\) промежутков одинакова, а сумма их длин равна \(ab+1\). Поэтому математическое ожидание равно
\[
\frac{ab+1}{n+1}.
\]

results.answer:
The board consists of \(a\) rows and \(b\) columns of unit cells, indexed by row indices \(i = 0, \dots, a-1\) (increasing upwards) and column indices \(j = 0, \dots, b-1\) (increasing rightwards), with the token starting at cell \((i,j) = (0,0)\). The movement is modeled by the positions at discrete times \(t \geq 0\):
\[
j(t) = 
\begin{cases}
u & \text{if } 0 \leq u < b, \\
2b-1-u & \text{if } b \leq u < 2b,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(u = t \bmod (2b)\), and likewise for the row coordinate \(i(t)\) with parameter \(a\) in place of \(b\). This model is consistent with the reflection rule described in the problem (in particular, it reproduces the given example of reflection at a vertical boundary, under which the token moves to the cell directly above its current position).

Let \(M = ab\) and let \(p_t = (i(t), j(t))\) denote the cell occupied at time \(t\). We claim that the cells \(p_0, p_1, \dots, p_{M-1}\) are all distinct (hence a permutation of the \(M\) cells of the board). To prove this, suppose for a contradiction that \(0 \leq s < t \leq M-1\) satisfy \(p_s = p_t\). Write \(x = j(s) = j(t)\), \(y = i(s) = i(t)\) and \(d = t-s \in (0,M)\). The times \(u\) at which the column coordinate equals \(x\) are precisely the terms of the two arithmetic progressions
\[
u \equiv x \pmod{2b} \qquad \text{or} \qquad u \equiv 2b-1-x \pmod{2b}.
\]
An analogous statement holds for the row coordinate and the value \(y\). Consequently \(s\) and \(t\) each satisfy one of the four possible pairs of congruences
\[
t \equiv \alpha_p \pmod{2b}, \qquad t \equiv \beta_q \pmod{2a},
\]
where \(p,q \in \{0,1\}\),
\[
\alpha_0 = x,\quad \alpha_1 = 2b-1-x,\quad \beta_0 = y,\quad \beta_1 = 2a-1-y.
\]
Denote these four cases by the pairs \((p,q)\). If \(s\) and \(t\) belong to the same case, then \(t \equiv s \pmod{\operatorname{lcm}(2a,2b)}\). But \(\operatorname{lcm}(2a,2b) = 2ab\) (using \(\gcd(a,b)=1\)), so \(d \geq 2ab\), contradicting \(d < M\). Thus \(s\) and \(t\) belong to distinct cases.

- Suppose the cases differ only in the row congruence (identical column congruence). Then \(d \equiv 0 \pmod{2b}\), so \(d = 2bk\) for some integer \(k \geq 1\). The differing row congruences give \(d \equiv 2y + 1 \pmod{2a}\). The left side is even while the right side is odd, and the difference is divisible by the even number \(2a\), which is impossible.
- The case in which the congruences differ only in the column coordinate is symmetric and yields the same contradiction.
- Suppose the cases differ in both congruences. Then
  \[
  t + s \equiv -1 \pmod{2b}, \qquad t + s \equiv -1 \pmod{2a}.
  \]
  Hence \(t + s + 1\) is divisible by \(\operatorname{lcm}(2a,2b) = 2ab\). Given the range of \(s\) and \(t\), we have \(1 \leq t + s + 1 < 2ab\), so necessarily \(t + s + 1 = 2ab\) and \(t + s = 2ab - 1\). But then \(\max(t,s) \geq ab\), contradicting the assumption that both lie in \([0,M)\).

All possibilities lead to contradictions. Therefore the cells \(p_0,\dots,p_{M-1}\) are distinct and the sequence visits every cell of the board exactly once.

The token occupies cell \(p_t\) after \(t\) steps and stops at the first time \(\tau \geq 0\) at which \(p_\tau\) carries a mark. The number of visited cells (including the final cell) is therefore \(\tau + 1\). Let \(S\) be the set of indices \(i\) for which \(p_i\) carries a mark. Because the sequence \(\{p_0,\dots,p_{M-1}\}\) enumerates every cell exactly once and the \(n\) marks are placed uniformly at random, \(S\) is a uniformly random \(n\)-element subset of \(\{0,1,\dots,M-1\}\). (We assume throughout that \(1 \leq n \leq M\), so that \(\tau\) is almost surely finite.) Thus \(\tau = \min S\) and the desired expectation is \(E[\tau + 1]\).

For a nonnegative integer-valued random variable \(X\) we have \(E[X] = \sum_{k \geq 0} \Pr(X > k)\). Consequently
\[
E[\tau + 1] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \Pr(\tau \geq k).
\]
Clearly \(\Pr(\tau \geq k) = 0\) for all \(k > M-n\). For \(0 \leq k \leq M-n\),
\[
\Pr(\tau \geq k) = \Pr\bigl(S \subseteq \{k,\dots,M-1\}\bigr) = \frac{\binom{M-k}{n}}{\binom{M}{n}}.
\]
Hence
\[
E[\tau + 1] = \sum_{k=0}^{M-n} \frac{\binom{M-k}{n}}{\binom{M}{n}} = \binom{M}{n}^{-1} \sum_{l=n}^M \binom{l}{n},
\]
where the second equality follows on the substitution \(l = M-k\). The hockey-stick identity asserts that
\[
\sum_{l=n}^M \binom{l}{n} = \binom{M+1}{n+1}.
\]
(To see this, interpret the right-hand side as the number of ways to choose an \((n+1)\)-element subset of \(\{1,2,\dots,M+1\}\). For any such subset let \(j+1\) be its largest element, so that \(r \leq j \leq M\). The remaining \(n\) elements must then be chosen from \(\{1,2,\dots,j\}\), which can be done in \(\binom{j}{n}\) ways. Summing over admissible \(j\) yields the identity.) Therefore
\[
E[\tau + 1] = \binom{M}{n}^{-1} \binom{M+1}{n+1} = \frac{M+1}{n+1}.
\]
Substituting \(M = ab\) gives the expectation \(\frac{ab+1}{n+1}\).

(Note that the assumption \(n \geq 1\) is essential for finiteness: when \(n=0\) the token never stops and the expectation is infinite. The problem statement is compatible with this range, as the uniform distribution over \(n\)-subsets is well-defined for \(0 \leq n \leq ab\), but the expectation is finite precisely when \(n \geq 1\).)

Final answer: \(\dfrac{ab+1}{n+1}\)

The board consists of \(a\) rows and \(b\) columns of unit cells, indexed by row indices \(i = 0, \dots, a-1\) (increasing upwards) and column indices \(j = 0, \dots, b-1\) (increasing rightwards), with the token starting at cell \((i,j) = (0,0)\). The movement is modeled by the positions at discrete times \(t \geq 0\):
\[
j(t) = 
\begin{cases}
u & \text{if } 0 \leq u < b, \\
2b-1-u & \text{if } b \leq u < 2b,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(u = t \bmod (2b)\), and likewise for the row coordinate \(i(t)\) with parameter \(a\) in place of \(b\). This model is consistent with the reflection rule described in the problem (in particular, it reproduces the given example of reflection at a vertical boundary, under which the token moves to the cell directly above its current position).

Let \(M = ab\) and let \(p_t = (i(t), j(t))\) denote the cell occupied at time \(t\). We claim that the cells \(p_0, p_1, \dots, p_{M-1}\) are all distinct (hence a permutation of the \(M\) cells of the board). To prove this, suppose for a contradiction that \(0 \leq s < t \leq M-1\) satisfy \(p_s = p_t\). Write \(x = j(s) = j(t)\), \(y = i(s) = i(t)\) and \(d = t-s \in (0,M)\). The times \(u\) at which the column coordinate equals \(x\) are precisely the terms of the two arithmetic progressions
\[
u \equiv x \pmod{2b} \qquad \text{or} \qquad u \equiv 2b-1-x \pmod{2b}.
\]
An analogous statement holds for the row coordinate and the value \(y\). Consequently \(s\) and \(t\) each satisfy one of the four possible pairs of congruences
\[
t \equiv \alpha_p \pmod{2b}, \qquad t \equiv \beta_q \pmod{2a},
\]
where \(p,q \in \{0,1\}\),
\[
\alpha_0 = x,\quad \alpha_1 = 2b-1-x,\quad \beta_0 = y,\quad \beta_1 = 2a-1-y.
\]
Denote these four cases by the pairs \((p,q)\). If \(s\) and \(t\) belong to the same case, then \(t \equiv s \pmod{\operatorname{lcm}(2a,2b)}\). But \(\operatorname{lcm}(2a,2b) = 2ab\) (using \(\gcd(a,b)=1\)), so \(d \geq 2ab\), contradicting \(d < M\). Thus \(s\) and \(t\) belong to distinct cases.

- Suppose the cases differ only in the row congruence (identical column congruence). Then \(d \equiv 0 \pmod{2b}\), so \(d = 2bk\) for some integer \(k \geq 1\). The differing row congruences give \(d \equiv 2y + 1 \pmod{2a}\). The left side is even while the right side is odd, and the difference is divisible by the even number \(2a\), which is impossible.
- The case in which the congruences differ only in the column coordinate is symmetric and yields the same contradiction.
- Suppose the cases differ in both congruences. Then
  \[
  t + s \equiv -1 \pmod{2b}, \qquad t + s \equiv -1 \pmod{2a}.
  \]
  Hence \(t + s + 1\) is divisible by \(\operatorname{lcm}(2a,2b) = 2ab\). Given the range of \(s\) and \(t\), we have \(1 \leq t + s + 1 < 2ab\), so necessarily \(t + s + 1 = 2ab\) and \(t + s = 2ab - 1\). But then \(\max(t,s) \geq ab\), contradicting the assumption that both lie in \([0,M)\).

All possibilities lead to contradictions. Therefore the cells \(p_0,\dots,p_{M-1}\) are distinct and the sequence visits every cell of the board exactly once.

The token occupies cell \(p_t\) after \(t\) steps and stops at the first time \(\tau \geq 0\) at which \(p_\tau\) carries a mark. The number of visited cells (including the final cell) is therefore \(\tau + 1\). Let \(S\) be the set of indices \(i\) for which \(p_i\) carries a mark. Because the sequence \(\{p_0,\dots,p_{M-1}\}\) enumerates every cell exactly once and the \(n\) marks are placed uniformly at random, \(S\) is a uniformly random \(n\)-element subset of \(\{0,1,\dots,M-1\}\). (We assume throughout that \(1 \leq n \leq M\), so that \(\tau\) is almost surely finite.) Thus \(\tau = \min S\) and the desired expectation is \(E[\tau + 1]\).

For a nonnegative integer-valued random variable \(X\) we have \(E[X] = \sum_{k \geq 0} \Pr(X > k)\). Consequently
\[
E[\tau + 1] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \Pr(\tau \geq k).
\]
Clearly \(\Pr(\tau \geq k) = 0\) for all \(k > M-n\). For \(0 \leq k \leq M-n\),
\[
\Pr(\tau \geq k) = \Pr\bigl(S \subseteq \{k,\dots,M-1\}\bigr) = \frac{\binom{M-k}{n}}{\binom{M}{n}}.
\]
Hence
\[
E[\tau + 1] = \sum_{k=0}^{M-n} \frac{\binom{M-k}{n}}{\binom{M}{n}} = \binom{M}{n}^{-1} \sum_{l=n}^M \binom{l}{n},
\]
where the second equality follows on the substitution \(l = M-k\). The hockey-stick identity asserts that
\[
\sum_{l=n}^M \binom{l}{n} = \binom{M+1}{n+1}.
\]
(To see this, interpret the right-hand side as the number of ways to choose an \((n+1)\)-element subset of \(\{1,2,\dots,M+1\}\). For any such subset let \(j+1\) be its largest element, so that \(r \leq j \leq M\). The remaining \(n\) elements must then be chosen from \(\{1,2,\dots,j\}\), which can be done in \(\binom{j}{n}\) ways. Summing over admissible \(j\) yields the identity.) Therefore
\[
E[\tau + 1] = \binom{M}{n}^{-1} \binom{M+1}{n+1} = \frac{M+1}{n+1}.
\]
Substituting \(M = ab\) gives the expectation \(\frac{ab+1}{n+1}\).

(Note that the assumption \(n \geq 1\) is essential for finiteness: when \(n=0\) the token never stops and the expectation is infinite. The problem statement is compatible with this range, as the uniform distribution over \(n\)-subsets is well-defined for \(0 \leq n \leq ab\), but the expectation is finite precisely when \(n \geq 1\).)

Final answer: \(\dfrac{ab+1}{n+1}\)

The board consists of \(a\) rows and \(b\) columns of unit cells, indexed by row indices \(i = 0, \dots, a-1\) (increasing upwards) and column indices \(j = 0, \dots, b-1\) (increasing rightwards), with the token starting at cell \((i,j) = (0,0)\). The movement is modeled by the positions at discrete times \(t \geq 0\):
\[
j(t) = 
\begin{cases}
u & \text{if } 0 \leq u < b, \\
2b-1-u & \text{if } b \leq u < 2b,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(u = t \bmod (2b)\), and likewise for the row coordinate \(i(t)\) with parameter \(a\) in place of \(b\). This model is consistent with the reflection rule described in the problem (in particular, it reproduces the given example of reflection at a vertical boundary, under which the token moves to the cell directly above its current position).

Let \(M = ab\) and let \(p_t = (i(t), j(t))\) denote the cell occupied at time \(t\). We claim that the cells \(p_0, p_1, \dots, p_{M-1}\) are all distinct (hence a permutation of the \(M\) cells of the board). To prove this, suppose for a contradiction that \(0 \leq s < t \leq M-1\) satisfy \(p_s = p_t\). Write \(x = j(s) = j(t)\), \(y = i(s) = i(t)\) and \(d = t-s \in (0,M)\). The times \(u\) at which the column coordinate equals \(x\) are precisely the terms of the two arithmetic progressions
\[
u \equiv x \pmod{2b} \qquad \text{or} \qquad u \equiv 2b-1-x \pmod{2b}.
\]
An analogous statement holds for the row coordinate and the value \(y\). Consequently \(s\) and \(t\) each satisfy one of the four possible pairs of congruences
\[
t \equiv \alpha_p \pmod{2b}, \qquad t \equiv \beta_q \pmod{2a},
\]
where \(p,q \in \{0,1\}\),
\[
\alpha_0 = x,\quad \alpha_1 = 2b-1-x,\quad \beta_0 = y,\quad \beta_1 = 2a-1-y.
\]
Denote these four cases by the pairs \((p,q)\). If \(s\) and \(t\) belong to the same case, then \(t \equiv s \pmod{\operatorname{lcm}(2a,2b)}\). But \(\operatorname{lcm}(2a,2b) = 2ab\) (using \(\gcd(a,b)=1\)), so \(d \geq 2ab\), contradicting \(d < M\). Thus \(s\) and \(t\) belong to distinct cases.

- Suppose the cases differ only in the row congruence (identical column congruence). Then \(d \equiv 0 \pmod{2b}\), so \(d = 2bk\) for some integer \(k \geq 1\). The differing row congruences give \(d \equiv 2y + 1 \pmod{2a}\). The left side is even while the right side is odd, and the difference is divisible by the even number \(2a\), which is impossible.
- The case in which the congruences differ only in the column coordinate is symmetric and yields the same contradiction.
- Suppose the cases differ in both congruences. Then
  \[
  t + s \equiv -1 \pmod{2b}, \qquad t + s \equiv -1 \pmod{2a}.
  \]
  Hence \(t + s + 1\) is divisible by \(\operatorname{lcm}(2a,2b) = 2ab\). Given the range of \(s\) and \(t\), we have \(1 \leq t + s + 1 < 2ab\), so necessarily \(t + s + 1 = 2ab\) and \(t + s = 2ab - 1\). But then \(\max(t,s) \geq ab\), contradicting the assumption that both lie in \([0,M)\).

All possibilities lead to contradictions. Therefore the cells \(p_0,\dots,p_{M-1}\) are distinct and the sequence visits every cell of the board exactly once.

The token occupies cell \(p_t\) after \(t\) steps and stops at the first time \(\tau \geq 0\) at which \(p_\tau\) carries a mark. The number of visited cells (including the final cell) is therefore \(\tau + 1\). Let \(S\) be the set of indices \(i\) for which \(p_i\) carries a mark. Because the sequence \(\{p_0,\dots,p_{M-1}\}\) enumerates every cell exactly once and the \(n\) marks are placed uniformly at random, \(S\) is a uniformly random \(n\)-element subset of \(\{0,1,\dots,M-1\}\). (We assume throughout that \(1 \leq n \leq M\), so that \(\tau\) is almost surely finite.) Thus \(\tau = \min S\) and the desired expectation is \(E[\tau + 1]\).

For a nonnegative integer-valued random variable \(X\) we have \(E[X] = \sum_{k \geq 0} \Pr(X > k)\). Consequently
\[
E[\tau + 1] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \Pr(\tau \geq k).
\]
Clearly \(\Pr(\tau \geq k) = 0\) for all \(k > M-n\). For \(0 \leq k \leq M-n\),
\[
\Pr(\tau \geq k) = \Pr\bigl(S \subseteq \{k,\dots,M-1\}\bigr) = \frac{\binom{M-k}{n}}{\binom{M}{n}}.
\]
Hence
\[
E[\tau + 1] = \sum_{k=0}^{M-n} \frac{\binom{M-k}{n}}{\binom{M}{n}} = \binom{M}{n}^{-1} \sum_{l=n}^M \binom{l}{n},
\]
where the second equality follows on the substitution \(l = M-k\). The hockey-stick identity asserts that
\[
\sum_{l=n}^M \binom{l}{n} = \binom{M+1}{n+1}.
\]
(To see this, interpret the right-hand side as the number of ways to choose an \((n+1)\)-element subset of \(\{1,2,\dots,M+1\}\). For any such subset let \(j+1\) be its largest element, so that \(r \leq j \leq M\). The remaining \(n\) elements must then be chosen from \(\{1,2,\dots,j\}\), which can be done in \(\binom{j}{n}\) ways. Summing over admissible \(j\) yields the identity.) Therefore
\[
E[\tau + 1] = \binom{M}{n}^{-1} \binom{M+1}{n+1} = \frac{M+1}{n+1}.
\]
Substituting \(M = ab\) gives the expectation \(\frac{ab+1}{n+1}\).

(Note that the assumption \(n \geq 1\) is essential for finiteness: when \(n=0\) the token never stops and the expectation is infinite. The problem statement is compatible with this range, as the uniform distribution over \(n\)-subsets is well-defined for \(0 \leq n \leq ab\), but the expectation is finite precisely when \(n \geq 1\).)

Final answer: \(\dfrac{ab+1}{n+1}\)
